How comedy clubs
really make money

lines.text: Comedy clubs aren't really selling jokes. They're selling drinks.
lines.say: Comedy clubs aren't really selling jokes. They're selling drinks.

lines.text: And that two-drink minimum is how many of them stay open.
lines.say: And that two-drink minimum is how a lot of them stay open.

lines.text: The Laugh Factory says it helps pay the comics and keep tickets cheap.
lines.say: The Laugh Factory says it helps pay the comics and keep tickets cheap.

lines.text: At Helium, ordering nothing still costs $10, or $5 per item.
lines.say: At Helium, ordering nothing still costs you ten dollars, five per item.

lines.text: Example: 200 seats at $20 is $4,000. If comics get 70%, the club keeps $1,200.
lines.say: Picture an example club: two hundred seats at twenty dollars is four thousand. If comics get seventy percent, the club keeps twelve hundred.

lines.text: Two $10 drinks each is another $4,000. At a 20% pour cost, the club keeps $3,200.
lines.say: Now two ten-dollar drinks each is another four thousand. Drinks cost bars about twenty percent, so the club keeps thirty-two hundred.

lines.text: And we do drink out. The average US household spent $643 on alcohol in 2024.
lines.say: And we do drink out. The average US household spent six hundred forty-three dollars on alcohol in twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: In 2023, $343 of it was away from home.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-three, three hundred forty-three dollars of that was away from home.

lines.text: So the ticket pays the comedian. The drinks pay the club.
lines.say: So the ticket pays the comedian, and the drinks pay the club.

post.title: How comedy clubs really make money: the drink minimum
post.ig:
Comedy clubs aren't really selling jokes. They're selling drinks.

Many clubs require two food or drink items per person; the Laugh Factory says it helps pay comics and keep tickets cheap.
Helium charges $10 ($5 per item) if you order nothing.
Example club, 200 seats: the club keeps $1,200 from tickets but $3,200 from drinks (at a 20% pour cost).
US households spent $643 on alcohol in 2024 (BLS).

Sources: Laugh Factory and Helium FAQs, BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey, bar trade benchmarks.
News and education, not financial advice.
Follow @financeprostv for money explained simply.
